questions.statement: Which word completes: "The guide ___ knows every vendor in the market"?
questions.context: A tour guide in San Jose shows tourists the central market.

options.text: who
options.feedback: who is correct because it introduces a defining relative clause about a person, and the guide is the subject of knows.

options.text: which
options.feedback: which introduces defining clauses about things, not people, so it cannot refer to the guide here.

options.text: where
options.feedback: where introduces a relative clause of place, such as the market where they sell fruit, not a person.

options.text: whose
options.feedback: whose introduces possession, like the student whose father is a doctor, so it does not fit with knows.

questions.explanation:
A defining relative clause uses who for people, which for things, where for places and whose for possession. Here the antecedent is a person.

questions.statement: Which sentence adds extra information about the quetzal with correct commas?
questions.context: The resplendent quetzal is a national symbol of Costa Rica.

options.text: The quetzal, which lives in Monteverde is easy to spot.
options.feedback: A non-defining clause needs a comma after which and before the main verb, so this version closes the clause wrongly.

options.text: The quetzal which lives in Monteverde, is easy to spot.
options.feedback: Without an opening comma this reads as a defining clause about the bird, and the extra comma after it is misplaced.

options.text: The quetzal, which lives in Monteverde, is easy to spot.
options.feedback: This works because a non-defining clause about the bird is set off by a pair of commas around the whole clause.

options.text: The quetzal lives in Monteverde, which is easy to spot.
options.feedback: Here which has no clear antecedent, so the sentence wrongly suggests that spotting the bird is the easy part.

questions.explanation:
A non-defining clause adds extra facts about a noun the reader already knows and is separated from the main clause by two commas.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option uses a relative pronoun correctly for the teacher in Heredia?
questions.context: At a high school in Heredia a science teacher retired after coaching the robotics team.

options.text: The teacher, which explained the volcano project, retired in June.
options.feedback: which with paired commas would make the clause non-defining and also refers to a person, so it is wrong here.

options.text: The teacher who explained the volcano project retired in June.
options.feedback: who is correct because it is the subject of explained in this defining clause about the teacher.

options.text: The teacher whom explained the volcano project retired in June.
options.feedback: whom is the object form and cannot act as the subject of explained, so this clause has no subject.

options.text: The teacher explained the volcano project retired in June.
options.feedback: Dropping the pronoun leaves no verb slot for explained, so the sentence breaks into two unlinked parts.

questions.explanation:
Use who as the subject of a defining clause about a person. whom only works as an object, and which is reserved for things.

questions.statement: In "The trees which line the riverbank were planted by students", what is the clause for?
questions.context: Cartago students planted native trees along the Reventazon riverbank last spring.

options.text: It names the kind of tree that was planted.
options.feedback: Naming the kind would need a noun such as native after trees, not a verb clause with its own object.

options.text: It explains why the students decided to plant more trees.
options.feedback: A reason clause would use because, while this clause has a subject and a verb, so it identifies instead of explaining.

options.text: It identifies the students who did the planting.
options.feedback: Students is the agent of were planted, but this clause describes the trees, not the people who planted them.

options.text: It identifies which of the trees were planted.
options.feedback: This works because which restricts the noun trees to a specific subset: the ones standing on the riverbank.

questions.explanation:
A defining relative clause narrows the noun that comes before it. Here the trees are limited to those standing on the riverbank.

questions.statement: His office is on the third floor. Which option combines both facts correctly?
questions.context: Professor Ramirez teaches geology at the University of Costa Rica.

options.text: Professor Ramirez, whose office is on the third floor, teaches geology.
options.feedback: whose introduces possession inside a non-defining clause set off by two commas, which suits this extra detail.

options.text: Professor Ramirez teaches geology, who his office is on the third floor.
options.feedback: who his office has no verb after the pronoun, so the relative clause is broken and the information is misplaced.

options.text: Professor Ramirez, who his office is on the third floor, teaches geology.
options.feedback: A clause with who needs a subject and a verb, but who his office is not a full clause, so it cannot work.

options.text: Professor Ramirez, whom his office is on the third floor, teaches geology.
options.feedback: whom is the object form and would need an object after it, so it cannot stand in this subject position.

questions.explanation:
To join two facts about a person, make the second fact a non-defining clause with whose followed by the possessed noun.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence uses whose correctly for the new gym?
questions.context: A new gym is being built next to the soccer field in Heredia.

options.text: The gym whose is next to the field will open in June.
options.feedback: whose must be followed by the noun that is owned, such as roof, so leaving it with only a verb breaks the clause.

options.text: The gym whose roof is still green will open in June.
options.feedback: whose is correct here because roof is the possessed noun and is still green describes that roof.

options.text: The gym who roof is still green will open in June.
options.feedback: who introduces a clause about a person, and this gym is a building, so who cannot show possession.

options.text: The gym where the roof is still green will open in June.
options.feedback: where introduces a clause of place, such as where the children train, not possession of a roof.

questions.explanation:
Whose shows possession and must be followed by a noun: the gym whose roof is green. Who and where cannot show possession.

questions.statement: Which analysis of that clause is correct?
questions.context: The teacher who wrote the exam is from Puntarenas and will move to Alajuela.

options.text: It is a non-defining clause, because it can be removed without changing the meaning.
options.feedback: Removing the clause would leave an unidentified teacher, so the information is essential and the clause is defining.

options.text: It is an object clause, because who receives the action of wrote.
options.feedback: who is the subject of wrote, not its object, and a relative clause is not called an object clause here.

options.text: It is a defining clause that needs commas on both sides to be complete.
options.feedback: Defining clauses about people take no commas, and adding commas here would wrongly add extra information.

options.text: It is a defining clause that identifies which teacher wrote the exam and takes no commas.
options.feedback: This is correct because the clause restricts the noun to one specific teacher and carries no comma at all.

questions.explanation:
A defining clause identifies which person or thing you mean, so it takes no commas. Removing it would change the meaning.

questions.statement: Which option is the best reason to keep the commas in that sentence?
questions.context: Monteverde keeps its rainy weather, which surprises many visitors from San Jose.

options.text: They mark the clause as extra comment, not part of the core fact about the weather.
options.feedback: This is the right reason: paired commas turn the clause into a non-defining comment about an already named place.

options.text: They show that Monteverde is the place where the visitors come from.
options.feedback: where would describe a place inside the clause, but this clause talks about visitors and surprise, not location.

options.text: They are needed because the clause describes a person rather than a thing.
options.feedback: The clause describes the weather, not a person, so the commas are not marking a shift to human reference.

options.text: They can be removed without changing which place the sentence is about.
options.feedback: Removing the commas would not remove the comment, it would only force the clause to become a defining one.

questions.explanation:
Commas signal a non-defining clause: the reader already knows which Monteverde, so the comment can be set aside.

questions.statement: What does the clause in that sentence add to the word bus?
questions.context: The bus that leaves Cartago at five arrives in Nicoya before dark.

options.text: It adds a comment that could be deleted with no loss of meaning.
options.feedback: A deletable comment would need paired commas, and without them the clause here is part of the core meaning.

options.text: It tells us where the bus is at the moment of speaking.
options.feedback: Place would need where, for example the bus that waits near the terminal, so this is not about location.

options.text: It restricts the noun, telling us which bus among many is meant.
options.feedback: This is correct because the clause selects one bus out of many, which is exactly what a defining clause does.

options.text: It explains why the bus takes that particular route.
options.feedback: A reason would need because or so, and this clause has its own subject and verb with no link word.

questions.explanation:
A defining clause without commas narrows the noun. The reader needs that detail to know exactly which bus is meant.

questions.statement: Which option rewrites this sentence cleanly without changing the meaning?
questions.context: The two students who won the national science fair did it in Cartago last month.

options.text: The two students which won the national science fair, they won it in Cartago.
options.feedback: which never refers to people, and the extra subject they turns one relative clause into two broken parts.

options.text: The two students who won the national science fair did so in Cartago last month.
options.feedback: This works because who stays as the subject of won, and did so avoids repeating the verb in a long sentence.

options.text: The two students, that won the national science fair, won it in Cartago.
options.feedback: that cannot be used between commas in a non-defining clause, and this clause needs no commas at all.

options.text: The two students whom won the national science fair won it in Cartago.
options.feedback: whom is an object pronoun, so it cannot be the subject of won in this defining clause about students.

questions.explanation:
Keep who as the subject, avoid commas around a defining clause, and use did so when repeating the verb would sound heavy.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why is that the wrong pronoun before the clause about customers?
questions.context: The cooperative in Guatacaste sells coffee that customers order online.

options.text: which is wrong because the clause describes a place rather than an object.
options.feedback: The clause refers to customers, who are people, so where is wrong here and which is not being judged on place.

options.text: which is wrong because the clause must have no subject of its own.
options.feedback: A relative clause normally has its own subject and verb, so refusing one subject would rule out almost every clause.

options.text: which is wrong because the antecedent is a thing but the clause refers to people.
options.feedback: This is the right reading: which refers to things, and here the customers inside the clause are people.

options.text: which is wrong because a relative clause can never follow the noun it describes.
options.feedback: Relative clauses follow the noun they describe all the time, so the position is standard and not the problem.

questions.explanation:
Pronoun choice follows the antecedent: who for people, which for things. The noun inside the clause does not change that rule.

questions.statement: Which option rewrites the library sentence so the clause becomes non-defining?
questions.context: The public library in Heredia lends laptops that students use for research.

options.text: The library, which lends laptops, is open until nine.
options.feedback: This works because a comma before and after which turns the clause into an extra comment about a known library.

options.text: The library lends laptops, and students use them for research.
options.feedback: Two joined clauses with and is a good rewrite of the meaning, but the question asks for a non-defining relative clause.

options.text: The library that lends laptops is open until nine.
options.feedback: that without commas keeps the clause defining, so this version still restricts which library is meant.

options.text: The library where students study lends laptops until nine.
options.feedback: where would describe a place inside the library, but here the clause describes an action, not a location.

questions.explanation:
To make a clause non-defining, wrap it in a pair of commas and use which. Then the information reads as an optional comment.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: In "The shop that sells handmade bags", why is that clause left without commas?
questions.context: My aunt in Liberia runs a shop that sells handmade bags.

options.text: Without commas the clause identifies one specific shop, not every shop in Liberia.
options.feedback: This is correct: the shop is narrowed to one particular shop, and removing the clause would change what is meant.

options.text: Without commas the clause adds background news that the reader may ignore.
options.feedback: Background news belongs in a non-defining clause between commas, so that reading contradicts the missing commas.

options.text: Without commas the clause explains the reason my aunt left the capital.
options.feedback: A reason would need because or so, and this clause has its own subject and verb with no link word.

options.text: Without commas the clause would be grammatically complete but logically empty.
options.feedback: The clause is not empty, it names the bags, so treating it as logically empty ignores real information.

questions.explanation:
A comma-free clause is defining: it tells the reader which shop is meant. That is why it cannot be treated as optional.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option best avoids repeating the noun after the clause?
questions.context: The road that crosses the Braulio Carrillo hills is closed on Sundays.

options.text: The road crosses the hills, and the road is closed on Sundays.
options.feedback: This repeats road twice in a short sentence, which is clumsy when a single relative clause can do the job.

options.text: The road, which crosses the hills, is closed on Sundays.
options.feedback: This works because the comma-free clause is defining and the subject appears only once at the start of the sentence.

options.text: The road that the hills it crosses is closed on Sundays.
options.feedback: A contact clause cannot add a second subject like it, so the clause ends up with two subjects and no verb.

options.text: The road is closed on Sundays, which the hills are steep that day.
options.feedback: Here which has no clear antecedent and the clause trails off, so the reader cannot tell what is being described.

questions.explanation:
A relative clause lets you avoid naming the noun twice: the road that crosses the hills is closed. One subject is enough.

questions.statement: Which version of the mural sentence in the context is fully correct?
questions.context: The mural that covers the wall in Barrio Amon was painted by local artists.

options.text: The mural, who covers the wall, was painted by local artists.
options.feedback: who introduces a clause about a person, but a mural is a painting, so the pronoun does not match the antecedent.

options.text: The mural where covers the wall was painted by local artists.
options.feedback: where introduces a clause of place, but this clause has a verb and describes what the mural does, not where it is.

options.text: The mural that covers the wall was painted by local artists.
options.feedback: This works because that is correct for a defining clause about a thing and it carries no commas in this version.

options.text: The mural whose covers the wall was painted by local artists.
options.feedback: whose needs a possessed noun after it, so leaving the pronoun with only a verb makes the clause incomplete.

questions.explanation:
For a defining clause about a thing, that is the safe choice. who and whose do not fit things, and where asks about place.

questions.statement: What is wrong with this sentence: "A nurse who cares for patients lives in Quesada"?
questions.context: A nurse at the clinic in Quesada cares for patients who cannot walk.

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because who correctly introduces the clause about caring.
options.feedback: who is already the correct pronoun here, and this version ignores the real ambiguity between the two verbs.

options.text: The problem is that who should be replaced by whom because lives follows it.
options.feedback: whom would be the object form and would need a noun after it, so swapping it in would not fix the reading.

options.text: The problem is only that the sentence needs commas around the clause.
options.feedback: The clause is defining, so it needs no commas. Adding them would only turn it into an optional comment.

options.text: The problem is that who reads as the subject of the main clause instead of the subject of the clause.
options.feedback: This is the right reading: who can belong to lives or to cares, so the clause should be reworded to remove the doubt.

questions.explanation:
A pronoun that repeats a subject creates ambiguity, as in who lives or who cares. Rewording with other or who is on duty fixes it.

questions.statement: Which option reports the same meaning without a relative clause at all?
questions.context: The team from Puntarenas trained hard, which paid off in the final match.

options.text: The team from Puntarenas trained hard because the final match paid off.
options.feedback: because would claim that the final match caused the training, which reverses the meaning of the original sentence.

options.text: The team from Puntarenas trained hard, and that effort paid off in the final match.
options.feedback: This works because that effort carries the second idea, so no relative pronoun is needed at all.

options.text: The team from Puntarenas trained hard while the final match paid off for nobody.
options.feedback: while would suggest the two events ran in parallel, and adding for nobody changes the result entirely.

options.text: The team from Puntarenas trained hard, and the final match paid off instead of them.
options.feedback: instead of them would mean the match replaced the team, which is not what the original comment says.

questions.explanation:
A non-defining clause can often be replaced by and plus a short noun phrase such as that effort, keeping the same meaning.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option correctly joins both of those facts about the workshop?
questions.context: A student from Grecia asked whether the workshop that starts at eight has space.

options.text: The workshop starts at eight, that has space, so the student should ask early.
options.feedback: Two commas do not create a clause here, and that cannot open a second clause after a comma in standard English.

options.text: The workshop starts at eight and whether it has space, which the student still needs to ask.
options.feedback: whether introduces a yes or no question as a clause, and this version leaves the sentence without a main verb.

options.text: The workshop, which starts at eight, may still have space, so the student should ask early.
options.feedback: This works because which plus commas makes a clean non-defining clause and the main verb is the finite may have.

options.text: Whether the workshop that starts at eight has space, the student asked in Grecia.
options.feedback: Fronting whether leaves no main verb at the end, so the question clause cannot replace the sentence on its own.

questions.explanation:
Join only clauses that match in tense and voice. A non-defining which clause keeps the main clause independent and complete.

questions.statement: Which option compresses the sentence best while keeping the meaning exact?
questions.context: The house that overlooks the bay in Puntarenas has a large solar roof.

options.text: The house overlooking the bay has a large solar roof.
options.feedback: This works because a reduced relative clause keeps the active participle overlooking and the subject appears only once.

options.text: The house overlooks the bay, and it has a large solar roof.
options.feedback: This is grammatically fine, but it repeats the subject twice, which is exactly what the clause is meant to avoid.

options.text: The house is overlooking the bay, having a large solar roof.
options.feedback: A passive -ing form after is is not standard English, and having after it would be a second dangling participle.

options.text: The house that the bay it overlooks has a large solar roof.
options.feedback: A contact clause cannot take a second subject like it, so the clause ends up with two subjects and no verb.

questions.explanation:
After a form of be, an active present participle can replace a defining clause: the house overlooking the bay has a roof.

questions.statement: Which sentence keeps the relative clause and is fully grammatical?
questions.context: The engineer who designed the bridge in Rio Claro left the country last week.

options.text: The engineer, which designed the bridge, left the country last week.
options.feedback: which is reserved for things, and the paired commas would wrongly present the detail as an optional comment.

options.text: The engineer whom designed the bridge left the country last week.
options.feedback: whom is the object form and needs an object after it, so this version has a clause without a subject.

options.text: The engineer whose designed the bridge left the country last week.
options.feedback: whose needs a possessed noun after it, so leaving it directly before a verb leaves the clause unfinished.

options.text: The engineer who designed the bridge left the country last week.
options.feedback: This works because who is the subject of designed and no commas are needed for a defining clause about a person.

questions.explanation:
Check three things at once: pronoun for the antecedent, its job inside the clause, and commas only for non-defining information.
